articles.title: 2026 NBA Rookies Already Looking Like Draft Steals
articles.summary: Expectations for NBA rookies vary depending on their draft slot and the team they end up repping. The vast majority of first-year players, though, enter the Association facing minimal to modest hopes.
articles.body:
Expectations for NBA rookies vary depending on their draft slot and the team they end up repping. The vast majority of first-year players, though, enter the Association facing minimal to modest hopes.

A handful of rookies who fall into that bucket have already blown those measuring sticks to smithereens.

"Relative to expectations" is the guiding force here. Top-10 lottery picks will not be considered steals, particularly in a draft class as deep as this one.

Perhaps that changes over time. Kingston Flemings of the Atlanta Hawks will look like more of a steal at No. 8 if the guards selected in front of him don't deliver.

For now, we want the guys who are turning heads right away despite being taken at spots that implied they wouldn't.

Nate Ament, Milwaukee Bucks (No. 13 Pick)

Nate Ament joined the Milwaukee Bucks with the potential to get somebody fired or earn them a lifetime contract. It felt as if there was no in-between.

Well, the 19-year-old is finding the happy medium. His touch and volume from three are a pleasant surprise, and a quintessentially slight teenage frame hasn't impeded his finishing around the basket. He has made more shots at the rim than Darryn Peterson.

The 6'10" wing's on-ball creation is TBD. He has flashed smoothness in open space, but shouldn't be saddled with handling the rock in traffic. He will have seasons in which he finishes with more turnovers than assists.

On the whole, though, Ament is boosting morale in Milwaukee with plug-and-play offense. And while he suffers from rookie-year spaciness when guarding away from the ball, he's turned in a few enviable defensive stands against higher-profile one-on-one scorers.

Trevon Brazile, Denver Nuggets (No. 35 Pick)

Cracking the rotation of a team angling to win multiple playoff series is no small feat. Trevon Brazile has already conquered it.

The 23-year-old has become impossible to deny even as the Denver Nuggets get healthier. He fights for every rebound, including at times against his own teammates. He runs the floor. His half-court cuts lead to dunks or defensive collapses that turn into open threes for someone else. He blocks jump shots.

Brazile has a ways to go on defense, but he's made some nice rotations around the hoop when the Nuggets blitz the ball. Three-point efficiency will be a swing skill, but he's willing to space toward the corners and fire away above the break.

Denver's secondary rotation desperately needed a shot of adrenaline. It got one with the No. 35 pick (courtesy of San Antonio).

Yaxel Lendeborg, Golden State Warriors (No. 11 Pick)

Yaxel Lendeborg is the second-most important player on the Golden State Warriors. Not for the future. Right now.

Listed at 6'9" and 241 pounds, he looks and plays bigger, with the dexterity and versatility of someone smaller. His drives are a vehicle for moving bodies, drawing fouls and dishing out assists. He leads all rookies in shots made at the rim and is second in total threes.

Conventional wisdom suggests he won't shoot over 55 percent on twos and above 40 percent on threes all season, especially with Stephen Curry sidelined for at least the next month by an oblique abdominal tear.

Then again, Lendeborg is shooting around 48 percent on twos and 41 percent on threes with Steph off the floor. The offensive packaging isn't contingent upon anyone. He's among the league's most efficient players on self-created attempts , according to databallr.

Party poopers will point to his age, 24, as proof he'll peak early. Whatever. Lendeborg is an outside All-Star candidate and the Rookie of the Year favorite. You're not supposed to get all that from the No. 11 pick.

Aday Mara, Oklahoma City Thunder (No. 12 Pick)

Aday Mara has erased any concerns that materialized during summer league. The Oklahoma City Thunder have surrounded him with real NBA players, even amid injuries galore, and he's emerged as an idyllic frontline complement.

Worries over his foot speed were premature. He has the gait to effectively run the floor and the coordination to navigate tight spaces in the half-court coming off screens. He is money around the rim off the catch. His layup package is a tad shaky, but he's got excellent touch overall—including a nifty flip shot.

Although general enormity serves him well on the defensive end, 7'3" superstructures aren't supposed to spin and rotate around the basket as fluidly as he does. Among 100-plus players who have contested at least 25 rim attempts , no one is surrendering a lower field-goal percentage than OKC's giant.

Mara would ideally grab more defensive boards for someone who doesn't spend that much time alongside another big. But his boxouts free up rebounds for the rest of the team, and he makes up for any deficits on the offensive glass.

Whether the Thunder intended to grab a frontcourt cornerstone at No. 12 is irrelevant. Even if they did, Mara wasn't supposed to actualize their vision so soon.

Baba Miller, Los Angeles Clippers (No. 36 Pick)

Baba Miller has quickly become a League Pass darling. And someone the Los Angeles Clippers need to play.

The 6'11" combo big is doing a little bit of everything at the offensive end. He spreads the floor, attacks closeouts and slips into empty spaces around the hoop. He will finish more lobs as time goes on.

Los Angeles might need to tap into Miller's playmaking. He has enough of a handle to be a grab-and-go option off rebounds. The 22-year-old tossed a live-dribble dime in transition to Gradey Dick during a Nov. 8 win over the New Orleans Pelicans.

We need more time to have a better feel for his defense. He can get foul-happy or caught veering too far away from the basket. But so many of his mistakes are the result of over-activity. That's easy to appreciate. And it helps that he's a chase-down block waiting to happen.

With the NBA stripping the Clippers of five first-round picks from 2029 through 2033 following its salary-cap investigation, finding value outside the first round will be especially important. Miller looks like a promising find.

Meleek Thomas, Cleveland Cavaliers (No. 34 Pick)

Meleek Thomas was born to get buckets. The 20-year-old doesn't care from where, either. Just about any spot on the floor will do.

Of course, it's Thomas' three-point efficiency that really pops. He is currently on pace to have one of the best high-volume seasons from beyond the arc in league history . It won't matter if that doesn't hold. He's ripping cord on so many of his deepies that he has enough room to withstand a slump and stay over 40 percent.

Thomas has also put down a bunch of gnarly looks from inside the arc. Those aren't his most efficient takes, but even just the ability to get off contested off-balance jumpers is its own superpower. Shooting at an above-average clip from mid-range doesn't hurt, either.

While Thomas hasn't shown much as a passer, his playmaking isn't DOA. The present makeup of the Cleveland Cavaliers' roster doesn't necessitate exploring that space.

At 6'5", his activity on defense is a nice surprise. Nobody will confuse him for a shutdown defender, but the Cavs haven't shied from using him opposite premier guards. Heck, knowing the stakes of this season, the fact that they haven't shied from playing him in general says it all.

Stats are accurate entering games played on Friday, Nov. 13.

Dan Favale is a National NBA Writer for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky ( @danfavale ), and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, co-hosted by Bleacher Report's Grant Hughes .

articles.title: Every NBA Team's Top 3 Trade Targets After 1 Month
articles.summary: The vast majority of NBA players become trade-eligible on Dec. 15. Fittingly, that is when speculation and chatter begin to crescendo. The time for us to start thinking about what teams should do and who they should target ahead of the Feb. 11 deadline was yesterday.
articles.body:
The vast majority of NBA players become trade-eligible on Dec. 15. Fittingly, that is when speculation and chatter begin to crescendo. The time for us to start thinking about what teams should do and who they should target ahead of the Feb. 11 deadline was yesterday.

We will prepare ourselves accordingly: with a fresh look at each squad's should-be wishlist.

Each mini list is built while accounting for team needs, directions, cap sheets and available assets. Names who aren't trade-eligible until December (or January) are fair game for this exercise.

Every team will be given at least one ambitious target to keep things fun. Ultra-ambitious targets will be sprinkled in whenever appropriate (or to prove a point).

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

One glance at the Atlanta Hawks' contract collection shows they're set up for a big midseason swing. Their biggest need is a primary creator. Kingston Flemings looks darn good and is already starting, but the offense remains too reliant on CJ McCollum. That's an untenable dynamic if you want to make a postseason splash.

Kyrie Irving comes with a pricey salary, but the contract is short-term. The Hawks can use his player option next summer to renegotiate a longer deal at a lower number. More importantly, he could lose a step or two and still be an offensive force. The shooting isn't going anywhere. He can play off other ball-dominant talent—including Flemings.

Jamal Murray straddles a similar line. He doesn't have Kyrie's handle or raw creation, but he's a better defender and can play off anyone. Though the three years and $161.4 million left on his contract are steep, bargain-bin deals with Jalen Johnson and Onyeka Okongwu give the Hawks this season and next before it becomes a real problem. Atlanta should cross its fingers for a Denver pivot.

Day'Ron Sharpe rounds out the board as a heftier frontline alternative to Johnson, Okongwu, Jock Landale, Zuby Ejiofor and an eventually healthy Mo Gueye. While not a shutdown rim protector, he brings good-enough rebounding, physicality and defensive mobility at a backup's price point.

The Boston Celtics feel like they'll wait until the offseason if they go buck wild on the trade market, but Trey Murphy is Mazzullaball Nirvana. His three-point shooting scales to higher volume and movement. He's a lob target in his own right.

A team-friendly salary through 2028-29 only heightens his appeal. The Celtics can match his salary without including Paul George if they're willing to ship out Mitchell Robinson as part of a (mega) package once he's trade-eligible.

Speaking of team-friendly, Scotty Pippen provides ball-handling, playmaking and defense on the cheap. He is owed under $5.5 million combined over the next two seasons (2027-28 club option) and would spare Boston from overtaxing George, Derrick White or one of the younger wings from too much on-ball work. Pippen's place in Memphis' pecking order is shaky even when he's available as well.

Naji Marshall remains trade-eligible after signing his extension with Dallas, where he's dabbled in oversized point-guard work. Boston needed outside-in rim pressure before moving Jaylen Brown. Marshall delivers that in spades. The Celtics have enough floor-spacers to offset his rickety shooting outside floater range.

Now isn't the time for the Brooklyn Nets to go all-in. Yet Franz Wagner is a worthwhile exception—largely because he's only all-in financially.

The Orlando Magic would be moving him under cap-sheet duress to get out in front of next summer's second-apron squeeze. Brooklyn has the financial leeway to build around a pricey power wing who's a net additive at both ends. His brother, Mo Wagner, is also Brooklyn's backup center.

Younger fliers should otherwise be the Nets' trade-market currency. Ron Holland II typifies the approach with "the dials all go to 11" energy and toughness. Unless he turns into a dead-eye shooter, his future with the Detroit Pistons is up in the air after they doubled down on the trio of Cade Cunningham, Jalen Duren and Ausar Thompson.

Yang Hansen hasn't shown enough at the NBA level to show what makes him special: passing, range and physicality. He's two impressive summer leagues in and on a Portland Trail Blazers squad with no fewer than two centers in front of him. Brooklyn has more room to plumb the depths of his game, even with Day'Ron Sharpe, Mo Wagner and Danny Wolf sponging up center minutes.

It turns out LaMelo Ball was important to the Charlotte Hornets' offense. Who knew?

Charlotte hasn't exhausted all its internal offensive-engine options yet. Kon Knueppel has barely played. Christian Anderson is a work in progress. For the time being, though, Brandon Miller, Coby White and Dennis Schröder haven't looked like a collective answer. The Hornets can and should branch out beyond hoping Knueppel is a panacea.

Mileage will vary on how aggressive they should be pursuing upgrades. Charlotte hasn't fallen out of the East's playoff picture, but the LaMelo trade always oozed gap-year vibes.

Franz Wagner runs counter to those vibes. If you harp on the jump-shooting warts, you'll miss out on the driving, finishing, passing and defense. He'll cost multiple firsts even if the Hornets are saving the wildly expensive Orlando Magic a ton of immediate and long-term money, but having Miller, White and Knueppel orbit everything he does is an instant cheat code.

Zion Williamson would give the Hornets a similarly different offensive access point without creating redundancies with any of their core players. He is second in restricted area volume while spending more time off the ball. As Sam Vecenie of the Game Theory podcast mapped out, Charlotte has room to put the rock in his hands more often. His rim and free-throw volume would do wonders for an ecosystem lacking both. He won't cost you as much as Wagner.

Although Terrence Shannon Jr.'s playmaking is often conflated with getting downhill at top speed, he has flashed live-dribble poise coming around ball screens and throws pretty good lobs. Moussa Diabaté would eat . Between having a year left on his rookie scale and not being as high-profile as Zion or Wagner, he's the direction Charlotte takes if it's looking for a difference-maker without catalyzing dramatic change.

The Chicago Bulls are clearly rebuilding. That is 1) surreal to write with a straight face and 2) puts them squarely in young-flier, distressed-asset mode.

Focusing on long-term fits at center remains a top priority, but someone who can guard the ball and is (much) better than Isaac Okoro should crack the to-do list. Under no circumstances should the Bulls be jettisoning crown-jewel draft picks, which might rule out everyone on this list. It still never hurts to ask.

Anthony Black has leveled up his shooting again and is headed for restricted free agency next summer. The Orlando Magic are expensive as hell and won't get any cheaper. Chicago has gobs of space under the tax and desperately needs some defensive oomph.

Are the Dallas Mavericks and Memphis Grizzlies worried enough about the long-term health of Dereck Lively II and Zach Edey, respectively, that they're willing to sell low to medium? I'm asking for Chicago's Swiss cheese defense.

Odds and ends are all that can populate the Cleveland Cavaliers' wish list unless they're moving a core player.

They are hard-capped at the first apron, from which they sit just $45,000 . Their largest matching salary outside the starting five is the sub-$10 million Sam Merrill. After him, it's Jaylon Tyson…who's on the books for under $3.7 million.

Justin Champagnie, Jabari Walker and GG Jackson II are each cheap enough for the Cavs to dream about. All of them can log minutes as a backup 4. Champagnie can sponge up reps at 2 or 3 as well and would be higher up on the list if he wasn't recovering from foot surgery. Walker can slide up to the 5 in a pinch.

Depth-chart politics are Cleveland's best friend for each of these guys. Champagnie and Jackson are ensconced in crowded wing rotations. Walker's usage could plunge if Philadelphia's frontline is ever kinda-sorta healthy.

Kyrie Irving is a fleeting answer to the Dallas Mavericks' lead-guard question, even if they don't trade him. Walter Clayton Jr. has given them good minutes, but they should still keep sniffing around other fliers.

Scoot Henderson immediately springs to mind. He looked like a somewhat trustworthy shooter before this season, who didn't need to dominate the ball. His athletic profile isn't what it should be, but he can still get into the paint and has a defensive pulse.

Guards galore in Portland, plus Henderson's impending restricted free agency next summer, could leave him on the chopping block. The opportunity cost of prying him away shouldn't be huge—especially if the Blazers are interested in any of Dallas' vets (Max Christie, anyone?).

Reed Sheppard shouldn't technically be available. The best version of him does everything the Houston Rockets' offense needs—most notably, drill outside shots of all types. Sheppard gets targeted on defense and doesn't play with a lot of offensive oomph inside the arc. Both flaws are liable to trap him in Ime Udoka's doghouse. His minutes are already down from last season with Fred VanVleet healthy and Marcus Smart in the fold.

Tre Jones isn't a good enough shooter to top this list, but he's the most proven option. A maestro of the mid-range, he adds genuine ball control, speed and standout vision in traffic. Getting him would immediately make life easier on Cooper Flagg and improve the shot quality of any Mavericks center. Dallas is also big enough elsewhere to test out Jones-Kyrie backcourt lineups.

Ball-handling that holds up under playoff pressure should be exactly what the Denver Nuggets are Jones-ing for. Tyus Jones is small and not an aggressive scorer. The DeMar DeRozan fit isn't looking so hot.

Ty Jerome doesn't promise nuclear athleticism, but he's an absurd shot-maker off the dribble who doesn't need to monopolize the ball. The Nuggets can play him with Jamal Murray, as he creates a much higher ceiling for the minutes without Nikola Jokić.

Giving up Cleveland's 2031 first for Jerome feels a little steep when he's in a contract year (player option). But he's the Most Improved Player favorite right now. Those don't come cheap, as Denver should be able to squeeze Zeke Nnaji's contract into the deal and/or grab a flier on GG Jackson II.

Kris Dunn admittedly won't bring much ball-handling, but he's a willing screener who defends with All-NBA hellfire for extended pockets. A Zeke Nnaji-plus-enough-sweeteners package could get the Nuggets out of the second apron if one of those sweeteners is a dispensable young player.

Jordan Goodwin belongs on this list if Denver thinks it'll get enough supplemental ball-handling from Christian Braun and Cam Johnson this year. His three-year, $19 million contract is a pittance. At 6'3", he spends equitable time defending wings and guards. Like Dunn, nobody's writing love songs about his jumper. He's at 37.3 percent from three over the past two seasons, as the Nuggets need defensive firepower more than offensive polish.

Gauging the Detroit Pistons' ambitions is difficult right now. Poking around Austin Reaves ahead of free agency suggests they're itching for a splash, but their actions imply they want to see whether more spacing, pl us improvement from Ausar Thompson and Jalen Duren, can fill the No. 2 score/creator void.

Detroit should abandon all patience for the right player. Deni Avdija is the right player. He can drive the offense or play off Cade Cunningham while checking the "big-picture 4" box. He is the player you put pretty much everything on the table to land—particularly when his salary is small enough that you wouldn't need to include Thompson (who's poison-pilled post-extension anyway).

Portland would be bananas to ship out Avdija now, but he's too cheap to extend. The Ja Morant trade makes it harder to renegotiate and extend him next summer. Who knows whether team governor/human weenie Tom Dundon is willing to back up the Brink's truck for his prize forward if and when he can. The private-equity thing to do is sell him off at the peak of his value.

After that, we revisit a greatest hit with Michael Porter Jr. He supercharges the spacing and offensive optionality and won't be a blockbuster asset drain, beyond matching salary with free agency on the horizon.

Naz Reid would be an even better fit if the Pistons want longer-term security. He is on the books through 2028-29 at under 15 percent of the salary cap, with a 2029-30 player option. His three-point efficiency has dipped this year, but he is shooting over 38 percent from deep on real volume over the past four years. While he doesn't need to dominate the ball, he has the reps as a creator to slide neatly into a second- or third-scorer role, depending on where Duren settles.

Yaxel Lendeborg's emergence thrust the Golden State Warriors into modest buyers mode. They shouldn't go buck wild unless a huge name becomes available , but they're competitive enough to see what Kristaps Porziņģis, plus other contracts and draft compensation, can get them.

Wendell Carter Jr. would immediately eliminate concerns at the center position. His defense is renowned for its versatility but has peaked at "Call me Daddy" during certain high-end matchups.

Orlando's financial crunch after this season should make WCJ gettable. Its current financial crunch and playoff hopes likely mean Golden State needs to find third teams to hash out a package.

Lendeborg blurring positional lines in the best ways possible cranks up the Naz Reid intrigue factor. The Warriors could play both with Draymond Green or another big. They could also just run a Naz-Yaxel frontcourt. Both Reid (sub-15 percent) and WCJ (sub-12 percent) add money to the future payroll, but their price points tilt toward team-friendly.

Isaiah Hartenstein rockets up the list if the Oklahoma City Thunder are actually looking to reorient their books. Serious injuries to Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace and Chet Holmgren have compromised this season. With Aday Mara turning heads, might they look to shed future payroll and restock the still-full-but-not-overflowing draft cupboard? If it means bagging Hartenstein's defense, physicality and IQ, the Warriors should find out.

Offense should remain the Houston Rockets' biggest focus even though they're slaying it on that end of the floor. This big board attacks it from different angles and to varying ambition.

Trey Murphy III is the "We're a contender and the time is now" home-run swing. The 26-year-old soups up half-court spacing without dominating the ball and can slot into the 2, 3 or 4.

Ryan Rollins could have feasibly claimed the No. 1 spot on this list if he were playing better or Fred VanVleet didn't look so solid. His shot selection can be spotty and he's not the cleanest ball-handler, but the 2026-27 Rockets, unlike the 2025-26 Milwaukee Bucks, are an actual basketball team. His biggest warts might correct themselves in a higher-stakes environment.

Rollins doesn't get picked on as frequently at the defensive end as Reed Sheppard and has shown more panache on his drives. Houston would have to contend with his free agency next summer ($4 million player option), but he should run cheaper than VanVleet is now.

The Rockets don't need much big-man insurance so long as head coach Ime Udoka keeps pulling Jabari Smith Jr.-at-the-5 levers. Still, Steven Adams isn't a billboard for availability. Jalen Smith's floor-spacing and rebounding are better safety nets than present-day Clint Capela. And at a $9.4 million price point, Houston should be able to game out his arrival without entering the tax.

Backup bigs and wings loom as the Indiana Pacers' biggest needs until (or unless) they prove otherwise. The former takes precedence because Ivica Zubac can't play 48 minutes per game and also isn't above getting matched up off the floor.

Jaylin Williams edges out Yves Missi for the top spot. Here's a list of every player averaging at least 10 defensive rebounds and three made triples per 100 possessions since 2022: Luka Dončić, Jayson Tatum, Kevin Love, Victor Wembanyama and Jaylin Williams. 'Nuff said.

Missi is wildly imperfect on offense but could suddenly develop quality hands and touch around the basket thanks to the magic of playing alongside Tyrese Haliburton. The idea of acquiring a center on his rookie-scale deal will appeal to a franchise nearly $6 million into the luxury tax and juggling an expensive core in the years ahead.

Well, not quite. J-Will would top the board if not for his $7.8 million salary. That's far from exorbitant, but incorporating him gets complicated if the Pacers are trying to shed $6 million in salary. It's more likely Aday Mara prompts Oklahoma City to trade J-Will than Indiana pays the tax.

Jordan Walsh can defend all over the floor and only makes $2.4 million this season. His extension was cheap enough at three years and $15 million that the poison pill provision isn't a huge hurdle. His importance to the Celtics is the bigger obstacle. He's started a lo t of games, so Indy would have to come in with a real offer.

Collecting first-rounders is standard rebuilding-team procedure. It's even more essential for a Los Angeles Clippers franchise that was just stripped of five future picks.

Scouring the market for younger projects is next on the board after first-rounders.

Taylor Hendricks might be a "third draft" guy at this point. He is playing more center for the Memphis Grizzlies, hitting the occasional three and making the most of his paint touches . The 22-year-old should be more than gettable with restricted free agency coming up. He's expendable with Cameron Boozer, Zach Edey and Isaiah Stewart in the Grizzlies' rotation.

Nikola Topić represents the opposite end of the rebuilding-team spectrum: a second-draft guy. Health issues, including a cancer diagnosis , and an absurdly deep Oklahoma City Thunder roster have pretty much zeroed out his opportunities. They already declined his fourth-year team option, so getting him shouldn't take much.

L.A. is an ideal landing spot with the Clippers in nothing-to-lose territory. There is some redundancy with the team’s other ball-handlers, but Garland and Wagler can play off anyone. The Clippers can worry about pecking-order problems if Topić turns into something.

Combo forwards and backup bigs should be all the rage for Los Angeles Lakers trade-machine enthusiasts. The problem? They have just one first-round swap and three future second-rounders to dangle alongside matching salary. Rookie Cameron Carr adds glitz to any package, but he should be off limits unless the Lakers are landing a member of their closing unit.

PJ Washington comes close to meeting that criteria. He fits like a glove next to Walker Kessler at the 5 when his three-ball is falling. Though he's not a defender who turns the water off, he can be moved up and down the matchup ladder. Head coach JJ Redick can even use him as a backup center when Kessler is catching a breather.

Assuming Carr won't be on the table, Los Angeles' best chance of landing Washington is more about the Dallas Mavericks. The Lakers need him to tumble further down a crowded frontcourt hierarchy.

Turning 30 this February, Derrick Jones Jr. remains athletic enough to check tough defensive assignments and get up and down the floor. He tends to hit juuust enough of his wide-open threes to remain in a playoff rotation.

Day'Ron Sharpe would be a huge defensive upgrade at the backup-5 spot to Sandro Mamukelashvili and the ghost of Kevon Looney. His passing has stood out this season. He's willing to try stretching the floor from three. Thanks to Sharpe's functional experimentation and Mamu's shooting and driving, the Lakers could play both bigs together rather easily in bench mobs. Most critically, Sharpe is top-end insurance against Kessler missing any time.

Ty Jerome's Most Improved Player push doesn't diminish the Memphis Grizzlies' need for backcourt pillars. Cam Spencer, Jaylen Wells, Javon Small and Scotty Pippen Jr. are all quality players. The Grizzlies need someone at the 1 or the 2 with the potential to really pop.

Not that they should be in a rush to make a big swing. That's why Shaedon Sharpe is at the top. He's going to miss a bulk of this year with a meniscus tear in his right knee. Even as they outperform expectations, the Grizzlies have the timeline to take it slow with him.

For all his defensive flaws, Sharpe offers bonkers shot-making possibilities. His off-ball movement has always stood out, although Memphis will want a higher-end floor general if it's going to nuke some of his more damning impulses. If the Portland Trail Blazers are looking to offload long-term salary to make way for a Deni Avdija renegotiate-and-extend next summer, Memphis is a logical trade partner.

Anthony Black has shown more as a ball-handler and shooter over the past two seasons and can effectively cover for Jerome on defense. The Grizzlies must be prepared to navigate his restricted free agency next summer, but his forthcoming payday is also why the Orlando Magic might make him available.

You're either smitten with Reed Sheppard's shooting and defensive playmaking or turned off by his slight frame and lack of on-ball gusto. Either way, boom-or-bust, he's a higher-end backcourt prospect than anyone the Grizzlies have now. The Houston Rockets should be on Memphis' speed dial even if the front office plans to keep free-agent-to-be Jerome (player option) past the trade deadline.

The Miami Heat have enough shooting on any given night, but they remain hard up for ball-handling that doesn't shrink the floor.

Cam Spencer would take care of that—and then some. He is a dead-eye shooter who can chaperone the offense through its half-court motions. Treating him as a be-all orchestrator gets sketchy, but Miami can divvy up the workload among him, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Davion Mitchell and Pelle Larsson.

Bake in a contract that has Spencer under team control through 2028-29 for less than $3 million per year, the Heat shouldn't be above sending out a first-round swap or even a conditional 2029 first.

Daniss Jenkins' shooting doesn't always extend to off-the-dribble opportunities, but he's a human fireball off the catch and a serviceable offensive steward. The Detroit Pistons' motivation for trading him would be to open up run for Ebuka Okorie and get out in front of Jenkins' foray into 2027 restricted free agency.

Ty Jerome is lofty AF. He continues to average over 25 points and five assists per game on holy-hell shot-making. The Memphis Grizzlies aren't moving him on the cheap—or necessarily at all. Yet, his player option for next season is cause for the #ToughTalk. He's 29. The Grizzlies are operating on a different timeline.

If it looks like Miami is avoiding the lottery, would Memphis accept a 2028 swap and a 2029 first attached to salary for Spencer or Jerome (and other money)? My gut says no on Jerome. That shouldn't prevent the Heat from trying—or upping their offer in whatever way they can.

Beyond targeting more future first-rounders, the Bucks have so many guys that they should consider taking on distressed big-name assets, just to see what happens. This approach also aligns with them not controlling their own first-rounder again until 2030.

Can they get Zion Williamson without having to give up a first-rounder? Or help the Orlando Magic shave future salary while giving up modest value for Paolo Banchero, a flawed 23-year-old who nevertheless fits the timeline and has an All-Star appearance and a smattering of playoff moments under his belt? Might as well find out.

If this approach fails, the Bucks should see whether they can lop off the two years and $57 million remaining on Myles Turner's contract after this season without having to give up picks.

Ending up with Kristaps Porziņģis (not planning to rejoin the NBA) or Jordan Poole would hollow out an already problematic center rotation. Milwaukee will live. This season isn't about banking wins. It could accomplish more with the flexibility those expiring deals provide.

Adding size off the bench would go a long way for the Minnesota Timberwolves. They don't have many places to turn after Joan Beringer and Trey Lyles.

Rasheer Fleming would be a dynamite fit. He is long, can defend a bunch of positions, has the potential to gobble up small-ball 5 minutes and likes to crash the offensive glass. His contract is highway robbery. He's under team control at a combined $7.4 million. Though he seemed in line for a bigger role with Phoenix this season, the Miles Bridges acquisition has left him six feet under in head coach Jordan Ott's rotation.

Jabari Walker gets to the rim, rebounds and can also move around the positional spectrum on defense. His importance to Philadelphia has skyrocketed amid frontcourt injuries, but he could get lost in the shuffle if and when Dominick Barlow, Adem Bona, Dean Wade, LeBron James and Joel Embiid are healthy at the same time.

Micah Potter hit some ridiculous threes as a member of the Indiana Pacers last season and grabs a touch more rebounds than you'd think. Portland has a trillion centers, leaving him behind all of them in head coach Micah Nori's rotation.

Everyone in this universe and 99.9 percent of all alternate ones agree the New Orleans Pelicans shouldn't be aggressive buyers. At the same time, if they're going to give the roster a fighting chance, they should transact like they mean it. In other words, trade for a frontcourt player who fits with one or both of Derik Queen and Zion Williamson.

Jaylin Williams' defensive rebounding and willingness to fire away from deep are a nice complement to both Zion and Queen. His $7.8 million salary over the next two seasons is an even nicer complement to the Pelicans' books.

Jalen Smith would be an excellent under-the-radar addition. He isn't the deadliest three-point shooter, but he takes and makes enough of them to pull defenses out of the paint. This is now the seventh consecutive season in which he grades out as an above-average rebounder on both the offensive and defensive glass. The cherry on top? Smith is having arguably his best year as a rim protector.

Aaron Gordon is the most aggressive name here. At his peak, he does almost everything the Pelicans' frontcourt would need alongside Queen or Zion: defend, space, move without the ball, etc. The rebounding might be touch-and-go, but hey, that's an issue in New Orleans now.

Gordon's path to the chopping block is the toughest to peg. He is mission-critical to the Denver Nuggets' apex form, but he's not having a banner season. That, coupled with second-apron concerns and the emergence of Trevon Brazile, might increase their willingness to have a conversation.

Andre Drummond and James Wiseman are worthwhile regular-season heir apparents to Mitchell Robinson and Ariel Hukporti, respectively. Whether the New York Knicks have enough depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns to feel good about every playoff matchup is a separate matter.

Moussa Diabaté and Dylan Cardwell check the offensive rebounding and defensive mobility boxes. Diabaté is in his contract year and could wind up being a rental, but Cardwell is under team control through 2028-29 for a combined $7.4 million. Both can log minutes alongside Towns—an option New York doesn't have with Drummond or Wiseman.

Luka Garza falling behind Robinson and Neemias Queta in the Boston Celtics' big-man hierarchy is the Knicks' opening to get him out of Beantown. Ditto for his impending free agency next summer. After drilling over 43 percent of his threes last year, he is another tall body who can play beside Towns if New York so chooses.

Garza doesn't have the defensive malleability of Diabate or Cardwell, but he's a stealthy second-chance creator. Through five NBA seasons, he has notched a career offensive rebounding percentage of 15.8. That mark ranks eighth in the entire league among everyone who has logged at least 2,000 total minutes.

Injuries to Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace leave the Oklahoma City Thunder in need of more perimeter bodies. They should take this opportunity to get bigger on the wings. Forwards standing 6'7" or taller were clearly on their brains anyway. (See: Their offseason offer sheet to Spencer Jones.)

OKC's acquisition of Nique Clifford proved what, not-so-deep down, we already knew: Executive vice president Sam Presti isn't shopping for red-carpet names. The Thunder will instead be pillaging through the "Cost-Controlled Youth" bin.

Will Riley showed plenty of moxie as a scorer during his rookie campaign. The efficiency wasn't anything to write home about, but he scaled to both on- and off-ball possessions. OKC has the infrastructure to paper over his defense. Prying him out of Washington shouldn't be too difficult now that he's barely playing.

Jaime Jaquez Jr. has become the obligatory inclusion for these discussions. It's not hard to see why. He can get downhill in any spacing environment and is comfortable generating his own looks from a dead stop. Unlike in past seasons, he's also making his threes this year. His placement behind Riley is related only to his upcoming restricted free agency.

Ditto for Tristan Da Silva, who will also be a restricted free agent next summer. He won't deepen the Thunder's shot creation, but he's drilling catch-and-shoot threes at an absurd rate. In lieu of on-ball initiation, OKC's offense should welcome someone who opens the floor for everyone else. Especially when he's 6'8" and not a defensive zero.

The Orlando Magic haven't ranked in the top half of both three-point volume and efficiency since 2011-12. That trend is on pace to continue. Newly minted head coach Sean Sweeney has them firing away (shout-out to Tristan Da Silva), but they don't have the personnel to deliver enviable efficiency.

Naz Reid tops the list if Orlando is willing to do something spicy. Its books are within striking distance of the second apron , but a package of Anthony Black and Wendell Carter Jr. cuts both short- and long-term payroll when factoring in Black's next contract. The Magic could also look at permutations using Jalen Suggs' salary.

Either way, they'd have to be comfortable with Naz and Paolo Banchero as the starting frontcourt. Even then, they'd need to get a reserve center better than Goga Bitadze and Nikola Vučević. Charlotte has Moussa Diabaté in a contract year. He could be folded into any deal if the compensation is right.

Luke Kennard is taking more threes per 36 minutes than ever and earns less than Bitadze. The Magic and their fans should be rooting for the Phoenix Suns to fall off the face of the earth and sell like crazy.

Deuce McBride is in a contract year, which technically complicates Orlando's situation. He's a more established shooter than Black, who, because of his size, will cost way less to retain. Acquiring McBride would be an excellent hedge against AB pricing himself out of town or the front office electing to move him in another deal.

Close your eyes and point at a Philadelphia 76ers frontcourt player. Chances are pretty high they're an injury risk…if not already injured.

As a result, Philly chases backup bigs by default.

The Sixers' options are limited unless they're willing to move Dean Wade or Anfernee Simons once they're trade-eligible. That shouldn't be off the table, but Wade's defensive malleability and Simons' shooting aren't facets Philly can just discard. Cheaper options will be their bread and butter.

Moussa Diabaté's offensive rebounding and two-way mobility are an upgrade over any true center the Sixers currently have behind Joel Embiid. His entry into 2027 free agency is a potential deterrent, but it's also what makes him gettable. For a team right up against the first apron that doesn't have much dispensable salary, his $2.5 million contract is also a spreadsheet thirst trap.

Charles Bassey was (briefly) a Sixer once upon a time. These days, he's connecting on 70-ish percent of his two-pointers and grabbing 30-plus percent of available defensive boards for the Golden State Warriors. If the Dubs start to crumble beneath the weight of injuries, Philly needs to blow up general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr.'s inbox.

Familiarize yourself with Karlo Matković if you haven't already. The 6'10" combo big can space the floor, sprint behind defenses in transition and operate as a lob threat. You'd like him to grab more boards, but he makes up for it by being really ridiculously cheap. His $2.3 million salary is both teensy and expiring. He won't have many suitors in free agency if things work out in Philly.

Imagine a world in which Devin Booker doesn't need to be the Phoenix Suns' top scorer and setup man. What a concept!

Locker-room calls for a point guard upgrade aren't unfounded . The Suns should probably try starting Collin Gillespie first, but whatever. They could still use an upgrade. Here's the thing: This team is horrific on the glass , too. Phoenix can't ignore that.

Landing Domantas Sabonis could address both playmaking concerns and rebounding deficiencies. Granted, he is currently a shell of his former self. The 30-year-old is posting the second-lowest usage rate of his career.

That only makes it easier for the Suns to pitch the Sacramento Kings on a deal built around Jalen Green, Mark Williams (trade-eligible Jan. 15) and no picks. (Special thanks to The Timeline Podcast 's Mike Vigil and Sam Cooper for workshopping this deal.) Maybe it'll turn out Sabonis is simply suffering from a severe case of Still-Plays-For-The-Kings-itis.

Darius Garland's scattershot health and performance shouldn't scare the Suns. They don't have the assets to be choosy. Garland's shooting, fidgety cadence in the lane and broader passing vision would make life easier for Booker and kick-start the play-finishing utility of Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach. Attaching Green's contract to another just about gets the salary-matching job done.

Dejounte Murray wants out of New Orleans , as the Suns are apparently interested . A straight-up swap for Green would work and is probably what Phoenix should do. Murray doesn't solve everything, but he's an upgrade as a passer and defender. Equally important: Despite an Achilles injury in his rearview, he has the track record of someone good enough to re-trade later.

Raise your hand if you thought the Portland Trail Blazers would need perimeter shooting over defense? If you, like me, have your limb in the air, congratulations on being wrong.

Nickeil Alexander-Walker is the "Why choose between shooting and defense?" option. The reigning Most Improved Player is disruptive both on and off the ball, downing 39 percent of his treys since 2022-23.

Convincing the Atlanta Hawks to move him will take a Godfather offer. The Blazers have assets to throw around. NAW's mid-level contract is attractive enough to toss at him.

Jalen Suggs' shooting comes and goes, but he's a defensive dynamo and probably an underrated passer. Payroll concerns are coming for the Orlando Magic— and they know it. Packages built around some combination of Shaedon Sharpe, Scoot Henderson, Robert Williams and draft equity might get them thinking. Doubly so if they want to keep soon-to-be-restricted-agent Anthony Black past this season.

Jaylen Wells is making minimum-contract money this season and next and routinely covers the other team's best offensive players. That combination is enough to overlook the shaky shooting. The Memphis Grizzlies shouldn't be dying to move him, but he's not far away from requiring a new deal (2027-28 team option) as they're in the early stages of a rebuild.

Assuming the Sacramento Kings aren't prepared to short-circuit their future for the instant gratification of chasing the 13-seed, they need to go full second-draft mode.

Bilal Coulibaly is in a contract year and doesn't fit into any Washington Wizards plan that includes playing two bigs. His offensive wheelhouse remains TBD, but he's a pesky defender across up to four positions.

Jarace Walker has at times found himself behind Jalen Slawson in the Indiana Pacers' rotation and is in a contract year. Both tidbits should be music to the Kings' ears. So, too, should the Pacers' historical aversion to paying the luxury tax, which they're currently in .

Tidjane Salaün has the physical tools to be...anything. A little over two years into his career, he's become a quasi-formless archetype. He did, however, make strides last year as a shooter and rebounder and should be a transition lightning rod.

Knowing the Charlotte Hornets already declined Salaün's fourth-year option, the Kings shouldn't have to twist their arm to take a flier.

The more you think about the San Antonio Spurs, the more you want them to get their version of peak Aaron Gordon: that combo forward who spaces, defends his butt off, can pass and cleans up enough dirty laundry around the basket to let Victor Wembanyama roam.

Actual Aaron Gordon is no longer Peak Aaron Gordon, so he's out. Onyeka Okongwu is a worthy stand-in. He shoots well enough to be interchangeable with Wemby on offense and has enough center experience to anchor units without him.

Owed just $33 million total this season and next, Okongwu is not breaking San Antonio's bank. Financially speaking, anyway. The assets they must pony up to get him are a different story.

Collin Murray-Boyles doesn't meet the floor-spacer criteria, but that's the beauty of Victor Wembanyama. He doesn't need his frontcourt partner to be a perimeter assassin. CMB's defensive activity at both the top and back of the defense is more important. The Spurs have the bandwidth to develop him on offense: plenty of guards to find him and lineups with enough spacing to let him mix it up out of the short roll.

San Antonio's opening on the CMB front isn't clear. The Toronto Raptors could use a point guard, so maybe there's a larger deal that sends CMB, Immanuel Quickley and other money to the Spurs for De'Aaron Fox and draft compensation. Maybe this could be a Carter Bryant-plus-draft-equity solo operation.

Without that combo-big type, Trey Murphy III would be divine. He isn't as imposing as Tobias Harris, but the Spurs are test-running Devin Vassell alongside the three guards. Murphy is an upgrade as an off-ball player and offers more size.

Everyone on this list would cost a pretty penny in assets. San Antonio shouldn't flinch. The Oklahoma City Thunder's last 18 months prove that no team is inevitable. The Spurs' title window is open now. They should transact like it.

Shooting and passing top the Toronto Raptors' list of needs. Kyrie Irving takes care of both while creating a filthy offensive trio with Scottie Barnes and Kawhi Leonard.

Aging up the roster even further would be a risk, as Kyrie's $39.5 million isn't cheap. The Raptors have two other stars to streamline his workload. They can use his player option next summer as a chance to negotiate a longer deal with a smaller annual number.

Jalen Suggs doesn't receive enough credit for passing. The shooting can be rough, but he hit 39.3 percent of his spot-up threes last year. He also upgrades the top of Toronto's defense, which is pretty terrifying. Ignoring his salary, injury history and start to this season is tough. They're not prohibitive enough to exclude him. If anything, his flaws and concerns stand to make him more attainable.

Jalen Smith is the mother of all "let's actually see Scottie, Kawhi and crew get to play together before we do something seismic" inclusions. He opens the floor from the 5 spot and is more active as a rebounder and rim protector than his reputation suggests. Toronto could play him in all sorts of different lineups, alongside one or both of Scottie and Collin Murray-Boyles and maybe even for a few beats next to Jakob Poeltl.

Believe it or not, Smith's $9.4 million salary is an issue. The Raptors' contract stash is more conducive to bigger swings. That doesn't make this a deal-breaker. It's more like a deal-expander. A package that nets Toronto Smith and a reunion with Norman Powell (trade-eligible Dec. 15) would be worth exploring.

Isaiah Hartenstein (trade-eligible Dec. 15)

Plunging to the depths of the Western Conference standings amid injuries shouldn't dissuade the Utah Jazz from being aggressive. They have a gaping hole at the 5. A healthy Jusuf Nurkić can't fill it forever. They have the assets to go big-name hunting.

Isaiah Hartenstein would be an ideal get for his physicality, rebounding, passing and trusty ol' flip shot. Utah can play him alongside Jaren Jackson Jr. without issue and doesn't need to worry about him griping if head coach Will Hardy deems it necessary to run JJJ at the 5 to close games.

It's hard to say whether injuries ripping through the Oklahoma City Thunder's roster make Hartenstein more or less of a pipe dream. Aday Mara looks like the real deal. Moving off Hartenstein's money eases the current and future financial crunch. At the same time, Chet Holmgren's injury history could preclude the Thunder from considering even the most over-the-top Hartenstein pursuits.

Get ready to hear Jarrett Allen's name mentioned a ton in Utah circles this year. He isn't the most imposing big, but he would boost the Jazz's rim protection and rebounding and does a ton of ancillary things on offense beyond finishing. He (probably) costs more than anyone on this list to land, so that's food for thought.

Onyeka Okongwu isn't a towering big himself, but his shooting, passing, and switchability are perfect for this Jazz roster. A frontcourt built around him and Jackson may not board every miss, but it'd be among the three or four most versatile defensive tandems around.

Wing shooting is easily the Washington Wizards' biggest pain point. It doesn't even matter anymore whether it comes at the expense of defense. The Wizards are bad at both ends right now. The dearth of knockdown shooting around a Trae Young-Anthony Davis tandem that often sees time with another big is madness.

Aaron Nesmith would decidedly not torpedo the defense—an added bonus that renders this an ambitious option.

Prying him away from the Indiana Pacers is an "over my dead body" undertaking. They aren't teeming with two-way wings themselves. The Wizards have enough assets to get the conversation started, particularly if Indiana doesn't exit the play-in territory.

Cam Johnson could become collateral damage of the Denver Nuggets inevitably getting out of the second apron. Washington should be among the first in line for his passing, shooting and overall feel if that's the case. He's not anchoring a perimeter defense on his own, but he's also not capsizing it.

Max Strus is an excellent stab-in-the-dark option should the Wizards want to play it safe. His $16.7 million salary comes off the books after this season. An extensive injury prevents the Los Angeles Clippers from demanding the moon. If the price is right, Strus' shooting and playmaking would be a functional godsend.

Dan Favale is a National NBA Writer for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky ( @danfavale ), and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, co-hosted by Bleacher Report's Grant Hughes .

articles.body: LeBron James, the former Los Angeles Lakers’ icon, and his wife, the popular entrepreneur Savannah James, have had a pretty perfect life ever since they got married. Their love and commitment to each other ever since they were teenagers has inspired a generation. Amid this, the NBA icon’s recent comments about a disagreement with his wife has sparked a heated debate.LeBron James makes a confession sparking a heated debate about his marriage to Savannah JamesA few hours ago, the 41 year old NBA icon LeBron James made an appearance on Steve Nash’s Mind The Game podcast where he opened up about his life and said, “My wife is pissed at me right now. We're building a house in Los Angeles…and she’s right to.”The Philadelphia 76ers’ star player added, “I f**king put like a little half court, little basketball court outside the workout. She was like, ‘We could have used that real estate for something else’.”The four time NBA champion continued, “It's gonna be a fu**ing hoop just sitting there for no reason. articles.title: La NBA Europa se atasca a 11 meses de su lanzamiento: no tiene equipos
articles.standfirst: Según un artículo de 'The Athletic', el comisionado Adam Silver admite que el producto inicial de octubre de 2027 será diferente al ambicioso proyecto que planeaban
articles.summary: Según un artículo de 'The Athletic', el comisionado Adam Silver admite que el producto inicial de octubre de 2027 será diferente al ambicioso proyecto que planeaban
articles.body: La NBA mantiene octubre de 2027 como fecha de referencia para poner en marcha su proyecto de competición en Europa. Quedan 11 meses y se antoja poco tiempo para crear desde cero algo tan grande y ambicioso como estaba previsto. "En términos generales, es improbable que se pueda lanzar una Liga seria". Esa es la demoledora frase de un miembro de un posible grupo propietario de una franquicia que recoge un artículo de 'The Athletic'. En los planes de la NBA estaba una competición de 16 equipos, 12 fijos y cuatro cuya plaza se ganara por méritos deportivos a través de las Ligas nacionales o un torneo clasificatorio previo. Básicamente, el problema es que ahora mismo no hay ningún participante asegurado. La iniciativa avanza, pero con el calendario apretando, todo apunta a que el lanzamiento tendrá que ser progresivo, con una primera versión que permita empezar a desarrollar el proyecto mientras se resuelven los numerosos flecos pendientes. El principal obstáculo sigue siendo la falta de acuerdo con la Euroliga. Las conversaciones entre ambas organizaciones se estancaron después de que a primeros de octubre, tras una reunión en el lago Como, la mayoría de los 12 clubes con licencia rechazaran una propuesta de la NBA. Desde Estados Unidos se pretende incorporar al menos a seis de sus miembros permanentes y ha llegado a plantear compensaciones económicas durante varios años a aquellos equipos que no consigan una de las 12 licencias iniciales, pero que abandonen la Euroliga. Las discrepancias, sin embargo, no responden únicamente a cuestiones económicas, sino también a rivalidades deportivas y a la distribución de poder en el nuevo escenario. Grandes clubes europeos como Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern, Fenerbahçe, ASVEL y Panathinaikos están entre los objetivos de la NBA y ellos han mostrado mayor o menor interés en sumarse a la competición. También se crearían franquicias desde cero en mercados estratégicos como Londres, París, Roma, Milán y Manchester. En enero de este año, 250 posibles inversores acudieron a una cumbre organizada por el comisionado Adam Silver en un lujoso hotel de Londres. Allí, 120 potenciales propietarios de equipos presentaron ofertas preliminares, lo que llenó de optimismo a la NBA. Sin embargo, aquel impulso parece haberse frenado con el tiempo. Las ideas no se terminan de concretar o al menos no se han comunicado oficialmente. Y sería importante airear cualquier avance para intentar acelerar el proceso y captar más adeptos. La Euroliga ha intentado blindarse ante la posible llegada de su rival: un sistema de franquicias, una ampliación del número de participantes... Ante las dificultades que está encontrando, la NBA contempla distintas fórmulas para su estreno en 2027: organizar un torneo clasificatorio con equipos de diferentes países, poner en marcha una competición preliminar con algunos clubes que ya hayan cerrado su incorporación, utilizar la Basketball Champions League de la FIBA como lanzadera... Silver y su vicecomisionado Mark Tatum, el que más está tirando del proyecto, insisten en que sigue adelante y consideran que la NBA Europa es una oportunidad única para transformar el baloncesto continental. El comisionado, sin embargo, ya admite que el producto inicial será diferente al que planeaban en un principio y que no tendrá nada que ver con el que finalmente se pretende instaurar. Hay mucho trabajo por delante para poner en marcha el torneo y parece que también se necesitará hasta que quede a su gusto.

articles.title: LeBron James sues makers of AI sports-betting app, saying they used his likeness and nickname
articles.summary: NBA superstar LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app Tuesday, saying they have deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing.
articles.body: NBA superstar LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app Tuesday, saying they have deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing. In a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in New York, James’ attorneys called it “a willful, bad-faith tactic” to use the player’s fame, likeness and nickname to promote “a new and unknown product.” The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using the Philadelphia 76ers star’s name, to give up any money they’ve already made, and to award damages — including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. “Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app,” the lawsuit states. “They intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions.” Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app’s website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday. The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc., is based in California. It was launched by Chief Executive Anish Gupta and Chief Technology Officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services like bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James — down to his tattoos, voice and number 23 jersey — sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app. James’ lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said. Gupta responded to the attorneys’ demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James’ legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app’s marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. “The integrity of NBA competition — and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play — is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views.”

articles.title: Grimes Joins Kobe in Lakers History, Top Box Score Stats & Highlights for Luka, LAL, Hornets Players
articles.summary: On a night when Luka Dončić recorded his 10th straight game with at least 30 points, it was Quentin Grimes who stole the show for the Los Angeles Lakers in their 118-114 overtime victory against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday.
articles.body:
On a night when Luka Dončić recorded his 10th straight game with at least 30 points, it was Quentin Grimes who stole the show for the Los Angeles Lakers in their 118-114 overtime victory against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday.

Grimes dropped a career-high 47 points on 10-of-14 three-point shooting in 42 minutes to help the Lakers erase an 18-point second-half deficit.

In addition to helping the Lakers win their ninth straight, Grimes joined Kobe Bryant as the only players in franchise history to make at least 10 threes in a game.

"I don't know why they left me open ... I don't think I would have left me open," Grimes told reporters after his historic performance.

The Lakers trailed by 18 in the third quarter and were still down 14 early in the fourth quarter when Grimes kicked things into high gear. He scored 21 points in the fourth, including the game-tying three with 1.7 seconds remaining to force overtime.

Dončić, who is no stranger to a heater himself and finished with 36, recognized how well Grimes was playing and made a point of getting him the ball.

Dončić actually brought his scoring average down with "only" 36 points, but he is still making history with his streak of consecutive 30-point games now up to 11.

The Lakers were able to get this performance from Grimes on a night when they didn't have Walker Kessler due to leg soreness and Austin Reaves is still out with a heel injury.

Los Angeles' victory combined with the San Antonio Spurs' loss to the Detroit Pistons moved the Lakers into first place overall in the NBA with a 13-2 record. They have yet to lose in the month of November.

A victory in their next game will give the Lakers their first 10-game winning streak since the 2019-20 season, which was also the last time they won an NBA championship.

Dončić and the Lakers will go for their 10th straight against the Utah Jazz in the second night of a back-to-back on Wednesday at Crypto.com Arena.

articles.title: Dylan Harper Injured Slipping on Court, Latest on Spurs Star After Loss to Pistons
articles.summary: In addition to suffering a 105-93 loss to the Detroit Pistons on Tuesday night, the San Antonio Spurs could be without Dylan Harper for a bit after limping off the court in the fourth quarter due to a hip injury.
articles.body:
In addition to suffering a 105-93 loss to the Detroit Pistons on Tuesday night, the San Antonio Spurs could be without Dylan Harper for a bit after limping off the court in the fourth quarter due to a hip injury.

Harper slipped on the court right as Stephon Castle was passing the ball to him and appeared to be favoring his groin area, but Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson said they were still waiting for more information on an official diagnosis.

"It just looked like he slipped obviously," Johnson said . "So, hoping for the best. But don't know anything yet."

Kawhi Progressing in Knee Rehab, Out Another Week

Harper was helped off the court and to the tunnel by Spurs teammates Keldon Johnson and David Jones Garcia. He went back to the locker room with the assistance of a team staffer.

Victor Wembanyama called it a "terrible feeling" seeing a teammate go down like that, but he is hoping for the best.

"It's a terrible feeling, terrible sight. I know as much as you guys, so I hope he's fine...But, yeah, I just hate this. I don't know how else I can say this," Wembanyama said.

Spurs guard De'Aaron Fox noted they were able to navigate things at times last season when players were out due to injuries, so they are set up to succeed again this season.

"At certain parts of [last] season we didn't have certain guys and what made us go is we were able to kind of cover for guys when they were out," Fox said. "So, right now, it looks like we might have to do that again."

Harper finished the night with 20 points and four rebounds in 35 minutes. The 20-year-old has taken a step forward early in his second season, averaging 18.4 points, 5.4 rebounds and 4.5 assists per game. He ranks in the top three on the Spurs in all three categories.

Tuesday's loss snapped the Spurs' 12-game winning streak after starting the season 0-2. They will look to get back on track Thursday when they host the Los Angeles Clippers.

articles.title: El Barça hace oficial el fichaje de Killian Hayes
articles.standfirst: El base con nacionalidad francesa firma hasta final de temporada y su contrato incluye una cláusula de salida para volver a la NBA
articles.summary: El base con nacionalidad francesa firma hasta final de temporada y su contrato incluye una cláusula de salida para volver a la NBA
articles.body: El Barcelona ya ha hecho oficial el fichaje de Killian Hayes, base de 25 años y 1,96 metros que esta temporada no ha encontrado hueco en la NBA después de que los Kings no hicieran efectiva la opción que tenían sobre él. Firma hasta final de temporada y en su contrato existe una cláusula para regresar a la NBA. Nacido en Florida pero con nacionalidad francesa por su madre, la exjugadora gala Sandrine Demiannay, no ocupará plaza de extracomunitario en la competiciones ACB, lo que supone otro detalle importante en su incorporación. Los azulgranas se han movido con rapidez para paliar los problemas físicos que tienen en posiciones exteriores con Kevin Punter y Umoja Gibson de baja y un Juan Núñez que no termina de coger ritmo. Este martes estuvo en el banquillo del Barça vestido de corto, pero no llegó a saltar a la pista en el partido ante el París Basketball. "Es un base que puede hacer el '2', un jugador con unas aptitudes físicas muy interesantes, que puede encajar bien con lo que tenemos y lo que estamos haciendo. Él estaba muy convencido de dar este paso y dejar atrás la etapa anterior", asegura Xevi Pujol, director deportivo del conjunto azulgrana. El nombre de Hayes ha sonado en las últimas temporadas como opción para regresar a Europa, donde se formó, concretamente en el Cholet francés. Este verano estuvo en la órbita de varios equipos de Euroliga pero, al no encontrar finalmente un hueco en la NBA, ha sido ahora cuando se ha decidido a cruzar el Atlántico. Hayes era uno de los agentes libres más cotizados que estaban en el mercado. En la máxima competición europea puede marcar diferencias sobre todo gracias a su capacidad física, que le convierte en un gran defensor y también por su visión de juego. Su principal hándicap está en el tiro exterior, que puede hacer que los defensores le floten y se colapse la zona. Habrá que ver su encaje en un Barça que hasta este martes sumaba nueve victorias consecutivas y parecía al alza. Tras crecer en el Chotel y jugar en el Ratiopharm Ulm alemán, el base ha pasado las seis últimas temporadas en la NBA jugando en los Pistons, los Nets y los Kings sin llegar a mostrar todo el potencial que se le intuía cuando fue seleccionado como en el séptimo lugar del draft de 2020. En 239 partidos en la competición estadounidense, Hayes tuvo medias de 7,9 puntos con un discreto 28,0% en triples, 2,9 rebotes y 5,0 asistencias. La temporada pasada sus promedios fueron de 5,5 puntos, 2,3 rebotes y 3,5 asistencias en 17,7 minutos a lo largo de sólo 23 partidos.
